source.title: Computation in Superposition: Two Handcrafted Models

record.file_problem: The post is readable, but some equations and displayed construction details appear blank or missing in the web text.
record.tranche_reason: The post tests toy name-pair networks and reports a trained subtractive mechanism that solves the task without the additive superposition mechanism, refining the claim that superposition is the only or necessary strategy.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the additive and subtractive toy-network mechanisms and their reported task results. The parameter-noise stability discussion is not a row because it measures robustness, not the claim versions. Some displayed equations and the full neuron-assignment details are missing from the rendered text.
record.test_reason: Trained toy networks on a sparse one-hot name-pair task, with more name features than neurons, often learned a collinear cancellation encoding rather than overlapping superposed directions. This qualifies V1's account of how small networks store features beyond their dimension count.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors say superposition is one strategy but not the only one. Trained nets used a subtractive cancellation mechanism, alone with two neurons or in a hybrid with six. They hypothesize that additive mechanisms matter when identity must be kept for downstream computation.
record.recipe_differences: This is not a reproduction of the original toy-model setup. It uses a handcrafted and trained name-pair classification task, and examines additive and subtractive mechanisms rather than a systematic sparse-feature superposition sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The post reports that the two-neuron subtractive solution was reliably recovered with negative score initialization; without it, additional help such as aggressive cosine annealing or minibatch noise was needed. It also compares two-neuron and six-neuron settings.
record.problems: The post studies a restricted toy name-pair task. The text does not give a systematic sparsity or geometry measurement, and some displayed equations and neuron-assignment details are missing in the web rendering.
record.rows_left_out: The qualitative parameter-noise stability results in Additional Observations were left out because they concern robustness of the subtractive solution, not a claim version. No other claim-relevant reported results were omitted.

untested.parts: No sparsity sweep or phase transition. No measurement of near-orthogonality or regular polytope geometry. No reconstruction-style task like the original.
All of V2: capacity competition and importance-based dedicated dimensions.
Polysemantic neurons arising without capacity pressure are not examined.

record.verdict_notes: Handcrafted networks are demonstrations of possibility, not evidence about what networks do, so they are unlinked. The task is a computation or classification task, unlike the original reconstruction setup, so the result qualifies rather than refutes V1. Whether the subtractive encoding counts as superposition (more features than dimensions, but collinear) is definitional; the authors say it 'sidesteps superposition entirely'. There is no quantitative report of trained-net weights; the evidence is textual.

versions.untested_parts: No systematic sparsity sweep or sparsity-dependent transition; no quantitative measurement of near-orthogonality or regular geometry. The post studies one name-pair task and describes constructed encodings.
The post does not test whether polysemantic neurons result from competition for capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
The subtractive mechanism is an alternative encoding, but the post does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise for other reasons.
No LLM representations, feature spread across neurons, or SAE recovery are studied.
No dictionary features or their completeness, stability, or canonical status are studied.
The post does not compare one-dimensional and multidimensional superposed features.

rows.subject: Handcrafted Network #2: The Subtractive Method
rows.size_stated: 2 neurons; arbitrary number of name pairs under the stated uniqueness constraint
rows.operation_detail: Described a two-neuron encoding in which paired first- and last-name scores cancel for famous pairs and yield a nonzero mismatch for other pairs.

conditions.value: No first or last name appears in more than one pair

rows.measure: Representation mechanism and number of neurons
rows.value: Two neurons suffice for an arbitrary number of pairs under the stated constraint; famous pairs cancel, while non-famous pairs produce a mismatch signal.
rows.note: The post explicitly distinguishes this mechanism from superposition: the classifier uses score cancellation rather than overlapping identity-specific activations.
rows.check: Handcrafted two-neuron construction; it shows an alternative is possible but is not a learned result. 'Reversed' overstates it.

rows.subject: two-neuron network
rows.operation_detail: Trained with two LeakyReLU neurons initialized with negative scores.
rows.value: The subtractive name-memorization behavior was reliably recovered.
rows.note: The recovered solution is described as the subtractive mechanism.
rows.check: The trained two-neuron net stores many names as collinear scalar scores, not nearly orthogonal overlapping directions. This is absence of V1's geometry rather than the opposite effect, so not 'reversed'.

relation.reason: The authors examine mechanisms arising in trained networks and report both hybrid and purely subtractive solutions.

tranche.reason: The trained networks provide a specific counterexample to treating superposition as the necessary encoding for this capacity-constrained task.

source_check.notes: This is scalar pair classification, not sparse-feature reconstruction; no sparsity sweep or geometric measurement is reported. The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased, and the downstream need for identity-preserving additive representations remains a hypothesis.
